title: Very short single-axiom systems for logic exist among the simplest axiom systems

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Very short single-axiom systems for logic exist among the simplest axiom systems

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Propositional logic can be axiomatized in terms of Nand by a single axiom with only six Nands (found by searching small axiom systems), far shorter than textbook systems, so an axiom system for logic is likely to be found among the simplest few thousand axiom systems.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: So what this means is that if one were just to go through a list of the simplest few thousand axiom systems one would already be quite likely to find one that represents logic.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 12, “The Principle of Computational Equivalence”; section “Implications for Mathematics and Its Foundations” (from p. 772), p. 809. Scope: equational axiom systems for Boolean algebra in terms of Nand

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch12-42: resolvable-now, resolvability 0.88

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Single-axiom bases for Boolean algebra are finite statements that public automated reasoners can verify decisively. Enumeration also tests the quantitative simplicity claim once the syntax and ordering are fixed.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Parse the proposed six-Nand identity, mechanically prove that it axiomatizes Boolean algebra with Nand, and exhaustively enumerate shorter identities to assess minimality and its rank among systems. A countermodel or failure to derive standard Boolean laws refutes the axiomatization.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Axiom length depends on notation and allowed variables.

The likelihood claim needs a specified ordering of axiom systems.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Short single axioms for Nand logic are a finite search plus a proof of equivalence, both standard, and both carried through for the six-Nand axioms. Model finders reproduce the screening step, and a formal derivation can check that a candidate axiomatizes propositional logic. The likelihood remark is then the position of those axioms in the same enumeration.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Search single equations with at most six Nands, test which small finite operators they allow, and confirm a survivor by a proof that it axiomatizes propositional logic. Finding such an axiom among the shortest few thousand candidates, and none shorter, supports the claim; a gap in the equivalence proof removes that candidate.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
The simplest few thousand depends on the enumeration order of axioms.

Allowing only Nand and Nor on a small domain is a screen; equivalence to propositional logic still needs a proof.

fields.label: Hypothesis
fields.value: If the claim holds, the published six-Nand single axiom ((a.b).c).(a.((a.c).a)) = c has exactly the models that Nand-logic has on small domains (on 2 elements only Nand and Nor, on 3 elements none, on 4 elements only the 12 operation tables isomorphic to the Nand of the four-element Boolean algebra); no shorter single axiom of the form X = variable passes even the 2- and 3-element screens; and in a natural enumeration of axiom systems by number of Nands a system passing all screens appears within the first few thousand.

fields.label: Method
fields.value: analysis.py enumerates every full binary Nand tree with k internal nodes and every leaf labelling over {a,b,c} (or {a,b}), builds the single-axiom systems {X = a} for k = 1..6 (34488 systems for k <= 5, 288684 for k = 6, 16896 two-variable systems for k = 6) and the two-axiom systems {X = a, a.b = b.a} with k = 4 (3402 systems), and screens each against all 16 binary operations on {0,1} and all 19683 on {0,1,2}; survivors of the 3-valued screen (and the published axiom) are then checked on {0,1,2,3} by backtracking over the 4^16 operation tables. A system 'works up to n values' if its models are exactly {Nand, Nor} on 2 elements, none on 3, and (for n = 4) exactly the 12 tables isomorphic to the Nand of the 4-element Boolean algebra. The published axiom ((a.b).c).(a.((a.c).a)) = c is rewritten with the variable on the right as (((b.c).a).(b.((b.a).b))) = a. Runtime about 11 minutes, of which 587 s is the 4-valued check of the 296 six-Nand survivors.

fields.label: Pass criterion
fields.value: Pre-registered. Enumerate all Nand expression trees X with k Nands (k+1 leaves) over variables a, b, c and consider (I) single axioms {X = a} for k <= 6 (34488 systems for k <= 5, 288684 for k = 6, plus the 16896 two-variable systems for k = 6) and (II) two-axiom systems {X = a, a.b = b.a} with k = 4 (3402 systems, 6 Nands in total). Screen each system against all 16 binary operations on {0,1}, all 19683 on {0,1,2} and, by backtracking search, all operations on {0,1,2,3}; a system 'works up to n values' if its models on each domain of size <= n are exactly the operation tables isomorphic to the Nand (or, on 2 elements, Nand or Nor) of a Boolean algebra of that size, i.e. {Nand, Nor} on 2, none on 3, the 12 tables isomorphic to Nand_4 on 4. PASS (supports) if (a) the published axiom works up to 4 values; (b) no single axiom {X = a} with k <= 5 over <= 3 variables works up to 3 values; (c) at least one system of family (II) works up to 4 values, and the number of systems of forms (I) and (II) with at most 6 Nands in total that precede it in the enumeration (fewer Nands first) is below 10000. The book's counts (0 of 16896 two-variable six-Nand systems up to 3 values; 296 of 288684 up to 3 values and 100 up to 4 values; 32 of 3402 in family II) are recorded as cross-checks and do not decide the verdict. If the 4-value search over all 3-value survivors of (I) exceeds 20 minutes it is applied only to the published axiom and to family (II), and the 100-count cross-check is dropped and reported.

fields.label: Fail criterion
fields.value: Pre-registered. FAIL (refutes) if the published six-Nand axiom has a model on 3 elements or a non-Boolean model on 4 elements (then it does not axiomatise Boolean logic), or if no system with at most 6 Nands in total passes the screens up to 4 values (then nothing 'among the simplest few thousand' is a candidate). MIXED if (a) holds but (b) fails (a shorter single axiom survives the screens, undermining 'as short as possible'), or if (c) fails only on the count bound.

fields.label: Unit
fields.value: six-Nand three-variable single axioms {X = a} (of 288684) whose models on domains of size 2, 3 and 4 are exactly those of Boolean Nand

fields.label: Interpretation
fields.value: Finite-model screening is a necessary condition for axiomatising Boolean algebra (every Boolean algebra is a model, and no 3-element algebra is), not a sufficient one; the sufficiency of the six-Nand axiom rests on the equational proof the book presents on pp. 810-811 (found with automated theorem provers) which standard tooling here cannot re-run. The test therefore checks everything about the claim that is checkable by enumeration: that the published axiom is consistent with being an axiom for logic on all domains up to 4 elements, that six Nands is the minimum passing even the weakest screens, and that a screen-passing system appears within the first few thousand systems of the book's own enumeration. 'Simplest few thousand' is read against the book's own ordering (by total number of Nands, systems {X = a} and {X = a, a.b = b.a}).

fields.label: Datasets
fields.value: Enumeration of Nand equational axiom systems with up to 6 Nands over 3 variables, with finite-model screening on domains of size 2, 3, 4, generated by analysis.py

fields.label: Caveats
fields.value:
Criterion (a) holds: the published six-Nand axiom has no 3-element model and exactly the 12 Boolean-Nand models on 4 elements, and every count the book reports for its search (0 of 16896, 296 of 288684, 100 up to 4 values, 32 of 3402) is reproduced exactly.

Criterion (b) as pre-registered fails: 8 four-Nand and 16 five-Nand single axioms over three variables survive the 2- and 3-valued screens (e.g. ((b.a).(a.(b.c))) = a). All 24 fail on 4 elements (they admit non-Boolean 4-element models), so none is an axiom for logic; the pre-registered 3-valued screen was too weak to separate 'passes a screen' from 'is as short as possible'. Under the 4-valued screen six Nands is indeed the smallest size with any survivor among single axioms {X = a}.

Criterion (c) fails only on the count bound, and only because the pre-registered enumeration order places every single axiom with fewer Nands before the two-axiom family: the first family-II system that works up to 4 values is number 1248 of the 3402 family-II systems with 6 Nands (number 1716 counting family-II systems of all sizes), but up to 36204 when all 34956 shorter single axioms are counted first. Whether that is 'the first few thousand' depends on the order chosen; the book's own text counts only the family it searches.

Finite-model screening is necessary but not sufficient for axiomatising Boolean algebra; the sufficiency of the published axiom (that it proves all of Boolean algebra) rests on the equational proof the book reports and was not re-derived here. Per the pre-registered rule, (a) true with (b) and (c) failing as described gives 'mixed'; every failure is a calibration artefact of the pre-registered criteria rather than a disagreement with the book's reported search results.
